The Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem for Normal Projective VarietiesThanks: Srinivas was partially supported by a Swarnajayanthi Fellowship of the D.S.T.

G. V. Ravindra Address: Department of Mathematics, Washington University, St. Louis, MO 63130, USA Email address: ravindra@math.wustl.edu and V. Srinivas Address: School of Mathematics, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Homi Bhabha Road, Mumbai-400005, India Email address: srinivas@math.tifr.res.in
Abstract.

We prove that for a normal projective variety XX in characteristic 0, and a base-point free ample line bundle LL on it, the restriction map of divisor class groups Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y) is an isomorphism for a general member Y∈|L|Y\in|L| provided that dimX≥4\dim{X}\geq 4. This is a generalization of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz Theorem, for divisor class groups of singular varieties.

We work over kk, an algebraically closed field of characteristic 00.

Let XX be a smooth projective variety over kk and YY a smooth complete intersection subvariety of XX. The Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem states that if dimension Y≥3Y\geq 3, the Picard groups of XX and YY are isomorphic.

In this paper, we wish to prove an analogous statement for singular varieties, with the Picard group replaced by the divisor class group.

Let XX be an irreducible projective variety which is regular in codimension 1 (for example, XX may be irreducible and normal). Recall that for such XX, the divisor class group Cl⁡(X)\Cl(X) is defined as the group of linear equivalence classes of Weil divisors on XX (see [10], II, §6). If dimX=d\dim X=d, then Cl⁡(X)\Cl(X) coincides with the Chow group C​Hd−1​(X)CH_{d-1}(X) as defined in Fulton’s book [7]. If Y⊂XY\subset X is an irreducible Cartier divisor, which is also regular in codimension 1, there is a well-defined restriction homomorphism11 1 The terminology is from the non-singular case, where one is considering restriction of line bundles.

Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y),\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y),

determined by the rule

[D]↦[D∩Y],[D]\mapsto[D\cap Y],

where DD is any irreducible Weil divisor in XX distinct from YY, and [D∩Y][D\cap Y] denotes the Weil divisor on YY associated to the intersection scheme D∩YD\cap Y. This may be viewed as a particular case of the refined Gysin homomorphism C​Hi​(X)→C​Hi−1​(Y)CH_{i}(X)\to CH_{i-1}(Y) defined in [7], for i=dimX−1i=\dim X-1.

Now let XX be an irreducible projective variety over kk, regular in codimension 1, and let L\script L be an ample line bundle over XX, together with a linear subspace V⊂H0⁡(X,L)\VV\subset\HH^{0}(X,\script L) which gives a base point free ample linear system |V||{\VV}| on XX. Let Y∈|V|Y\in|{\VV}| be a general element of this linear system; by Bertini’s theorem, we have Ys​i​n​g=Y∩Xs​i​n​gY_{sing}=Y\cap X_{sing}. In this context, our main result is the following, which is an analogue of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem.

Theorem 1.

In the above situation, for a dense Zariski open set of Y∈|V|Y\in|{\VV}|, the restriction map

Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y)

is an isomorphism, if dimX≥4\dim X\geq 4, and is injective, with finitely generated cokernel, if dimX=3\dim X=3.

Our proof is purely algebraic, in the style of the proof of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem given in [11], Chapter IV. The above result has an application in the theory of Deligne’s 1-motives (see [4]), which is discussed in §4 below; for this, it is of interest to have such an algebraic proof. In an appendix, we also sketch a different, transcendental proof of the theorem, when k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, due to N. Fakhruddin, using results from stratified Morse theory, and properties of the weight filtration on cohomology.

We would like to thank the referee for a critical reading of the paper, and detailed suggestions for improvement, including the discussion in §5.

1. The Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem for big linear systems

In the situation of Theorem 1, if X~→𝜋X\widetilde{X}\xrightarrow{\pi}X is a desingularisation of XX, we have the following (Cartesian) diagram:

Y~↪X~↓↓Y↪X\begin{array}[]{ccc}\widetilde{Y}&\hookrightarrow&\widetilde{X}\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow\\ Y&\hookrightarrow&X\\ \end{array}

Note that Y~\widetilde{Y} is a general member of the pull-back linear system π∗​V\pi^{\ast}\VV on the smooth proper variety X~\widetilde{X}, and therefore is smooth, by Bertini’s theorem; hence Y~→Y\widetilde{Y}\to Y is a desingularisation of YY. If XX is singular, then Y~\widetilde{Y} is a general member of the linear system determined by π∗​V⊂H0⁡(X~,π∗​L)\pi^{\ast}V\subset\HH^{0}(\widetilde{X},\pi^{\ast}\script L) where π∗​L\pi^{\ast}\script L is not ample, but is big and base-point free.

Let EX=π−1​(Xs​i​n​g)⊂X~E_{X}=\pi^{-1}(X_{sing})\subset\widetilde{X} be the exceptional locus. Then EY=EX∩Y~E_{Y}=E_{X}\cap\widetilde{Y} is the exceptional locus for Y~→Y\widetilde{Y}\to Y. We have natural isomorphisms

Cl⁡(X)≅Cl⁡(X∖Xs​i​n​g)≅Pic⁡(X∖Xs​i​n​g)≅Pic⁡(X~∖EX),\Cl(X)\cong\Cl(X\setminus X_{sing})\cong\Pic(X\setminus X_{sing})\cong\Pic(\widetilde{X}\setminus E_{X}),
Cl⁡(Y)≅Cl⁡(Y∖Ys​i​n​g)≅Pic⁡(Y∖Ys​i​n​g)≅Pic⁡(Y~∖EY).\Cl(Y)\cong\Cl(Y\setminus Y_{sing})\cong\Pic(Y\setminus Y_{sing})\cong\Pic(\widetilde{Y}\setminus E_{Y}).

This is because (i) the divisor class group is unchanged upon removal of a closed subset of codimension ≥2\geq 2, and (ii) the divisor class group coincides with the Picard group, for non-singular varieties. Thus, Theorem 1 may be viewed as an assertion about the natural restriction homomophism

Pic⁡(X~∖EX)→Pic⁡(Y~∖EY).\Pic(\widetilde{X}\setminus E_{X})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}\setminus E_{Y}).

Also, by a standard argument (repeated below), Pic⁡(X~)→Pic⁡(X~∖EX)\Pic(\widetilde{X})\to\Pic(\widetilde{X}\setminus E_{X}) is surjective, with kernel isomorphic to the free abelian group on the irreducible divisorial components of EXE_{X}, and a similar assertion holds for Pic⁡(Y~)→Pic⁡(Y~∖EY)\Pic(\widetilde{Y})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}\setminus E_{Y}). Indeed, since X~\widetilde{X}, Y~\widetilde{Y} are non-singular, any line bundle on any Zariski open subset extends to a line bundle on the variety, so the two restriction maps are surjective, with kernel given by the line bundles associated to divisors with support in EXE_{X} and EYE_{Y} respectively. However, if EE is any non-zero divisor on X~\widetilde{X} with support in EXE_{X}, then 𝒪X~​(E){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(E) is a non-trivial line bundle: if not, we would have a non-constant rational function ff on X~\widetilde{X} with divisor EE; then ff determines a non-zero regular function on X∖Xs​i​n​gX\setminus X_{sing}, which must extend to a regular function on the normalization XnX_{n} of XX. But XnX_{n} is an irreducible projective variety, so any global regular function on it is constant, which is a contradiction. This argument applies to Y~\widetilde{Y} as well.

Thus, Theorem 1 is a consequence of the following version of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem for a big and base-point free linear system, describing the kernel and cokernel of the restiction map on Picard groups, for the inclusion Y~↪X~\widetilde{Y}\hookrightarrow\widetilde{X} of a general member of the linear system. The statement is a perhaps a bit technical, but there is an obvious geometric motivation for the conditions stated.

Theorem 2.

Let X~\widetilde{X} be a non-singular projective kk-variety, M\script M a big invertible sheaf, V⊂H0​(X~,M)\VV\subset H^{0}(\widetilde{X},\script M) a kk-subspace giving a base-point free linear system on X~\widetilde{X}. Let φ:X~→ℙkN\varphi:\widetilde{X}\to{\mathbb{P}}^{N}_{k} be the morphism determined by |V||\VV|, and X~→𝜋X→ℙkN\widetilde{X}\xrightarrow{\pi}X\to{\mathbb{P}}^{N}_{k} be the Stein factorization of φ\varphi. Suppose dimX~≥3\dim\widetilde{X}\geq 3. Then for a Zariski open subset of divisors Y~∈|V|\widetilde{Y}\in|\VV|, the restriction map

ρ:Pic⁡(X~)→Pic⁡(Y~)\rho:\Pic(\widetilde{X})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y})

has the following properties.

  1. (a)

    ρ\rho has kernel (freely) generated by the classes of the irreducible divisors E⊂X~E\subset\widetilde{X} with dimπ⁡(E)=0\dim\pi(E)=0, and ρ\rho has a finitely generated cokernel.

  2. (b)

    If FF is a divisor on Y~\widetilde{Y} supported in EYE_{Y}, such that 𝒪Y~​(F)∈image​Pic⁡(X~){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(F)\in{\rm image}\,\Pic(\widetilde{X}), then there is a divisor EE on X~\widetilde{X} supported in EXE_{X} with 𝒪X~​(E)⊗𝒪Y~≅𝒪Y~​(F){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(E)\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(F).

  3. (c)

    If dimX~≥4\dim\widetilde{X}\geq 4, then the classes of 𝒪Y~​(E){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(E), with EE supported in EYE_{Y}, generate Coker⁡(ρ)\coker(\rho).

2. Some lemmas on vanishing of cohomology

Next, we collect together some technical lemmas, used in the proof of Theorem 2.

We first state a lemma due to Grothendieck (see [9, 13]).

Lemma 2.1 (Artin-Rees formula).

Let f:V→Wf:V\to W be a proper morphism of Noetherian schemes, F\script F a coherent sheaf on VV, ℐ⊂𝒪W\mathcal{I}\subset{\mathcal{O}}_{W} a coherent ideal sheaf, and 𝒥=f−1​ℐ.𝒪W\mathcal{J}=f^{-1}\mathcal{I}.{\mathcal{O}}_{W} the inverse image ideal sheaf on VV. There exists n0≥0n_{0}\geq 0 such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, the natural map

ℐn−n0⊗Ri⁡f∗​(𝒥n0​F)→Ri⁡f∗​(𝒥n​F)\mathcal{I}^{n-n_{0}}\otimes\RR^{i}f_{\ast}(\mathcal{J}^{n_{0}}\script F)\to\RR^{i}f_{\ast}(\mathcal{J}^{n}\script F)

is a surjection.

Here, 𝒥n​ℱ\mathcal{J}^{n}\mathcal{F} denotes the image of the multiplication map 𝒥n⊗ℱ→ℱ\mathcal{J}^{n}\otimes\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}.

Lemma 2.2.

Let W~→𝜋W\widetilde{W}\xrightarrow{\pi}W be a proper surjective morphism, where W~\widetilde{W} is an irreducible non-singular variety of dimension dd, and dimW≥2\dim W\geq 2. Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a coherent sheaf on W~\widetilde{W}, with Rd−1​π∗​ℱ≠0R^{d-1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}\neq 0. Then there exists an effective divisor E⊂W~E\subset\widetilde{W} whose support has 0-dimensional image under π\pi, such that Rd−1⁡π∗​ℱ​(−E)→Rd−1⁡π∗​ℱ\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{F}(-E)\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{F} is the zero map.

Proof.

Let S⊂WS\subset W be the support of Rd−1⁡π∗​ℱ\RR^{d-1}\pi_{*}\mathcal{F}. Then SS consists of points w∈Ww\in W with dimπ−1​(w)≥d−1\dim\pi^{-1}(w)\geq d-1, and under our hypotheses, this forces dimS=0\dim S=0.

Let ℐ⊂𝒪W\mathcal{I}\subset{\mathcal{O}}_{W} be the ideal sheaf of SS, and let

𝒥=image⁡(π∗​ℐ→𝒪W~)\mathcal{J}={\rm image}\,\left(\pi^{*}\mathcal{I}\to{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}}\right)

be the inverse image ideal sheaf in 𝒪W~{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}}. Lemma 2.1 above implies that there exists an m0≥0m_{0}\geq 0 such that the map

ℐm−m0⊗Rd−1⁡π∗​(𝒥m0​ℱ)→Rd−1⁡π∗​(𝒥m​ℱ)\mathcal{I}^{m-m_{0}}\otimes\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{J}^{m_{0}}\mathcal{F})\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{J}^{m}\mathcal{F})

is a surjection.

We claim that, for large enough mm, the map Rd−1⁡π∗​(𝒥m​ℱ)→Rd−1⁡π∗​(ℱ)\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{J}^{m}\mathcal{F})\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{F}) is the zero map. This is because by Lemma 2.1, we have a diagram

where the top horizontal arrow is surjective. The bottom horizontal map is 0, if mm is large enough, since ℐ\mathcal{I} is the ideal defining the support of Rd−1⁡π∗​(ℱ)\RR^{d-1}\pi_{*}(\mathcal{F}); hence the right vertical arrow is 0.

Since W~\widetilde{W} is non-singular, there exists an effective (Cartier) divisor E0E_{0} in W~\widetilde{W} such that 𝒥=𝒪W~​(−E0)⊗J\mathcal{J}={\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}}(-E_{0})\otimes J, where J⊂𝒪W~J\subset{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}} defines a subscheme of codimension ≥2\geq 2. In particular, we have inclusions of ideal sheaves 𝒥m⊂𝒪W~​(−m​E0)⊂𝒪W~\mathcal{J}^{m}\subset{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}}(-mE_{0})\subset{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}}.

Now consider the exact sequence

0→𝒥m​ℱ→ℱ⁡(−m​E0)→ℱ⁡(−m​E0)⊗𝒪m​Z→00\to\mathcal{J}^{m}\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}(-mE_{0})\to\mathcal{F}(-mE_{0})\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{mZ}\to 0

Here m​Z⊂W~mZ\subset\widetilde{W} is the subscheme defined by the ideal sheaf Jm⊂𝒪W~J^{m}\subset{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}}. This gives a long exact sequence

Rd−1π∗(𝒥mℱ)→Rd−1π∗(ℱ(−mE0))→Rd−1π∗(ℱ(−mE)|mZ)\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{J}^{m}\mathcal{F})\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{F}(-mE_{0}))\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{F}(-mE)_{|{mZ}})

We note that the last term is zero since the codimension of ZZ in W~\widetilde{W} is ≥2\geq 2. Hence the first arrow is a surjection.

To conclude the proof of the lemma, we note that the (zero) map Rd−1⁡π∗​(𝒥m​ℱ)→Rd−1⁡π∗​(ℱ)\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{J}^{m}\mathcal{F})\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{F}) factors as

Rd−1⁡π∗​(𝒥m​ℱ)→Rd−1⁡π∗​(ℱ⁡(−m​E0))→Rd−1⁡π∗​(ℱ).\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}({\mathcal{J}^{m}}\mathcal{F})\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{F}(-mE_{0}))\to\RR^{d-1}\pi_{\ast}(\mathcal{F}).

Since the first map is a surjection, the second is necessarily the zero map. The lemma thus holds with E=m​E0E=mE_{0}, where mm is sufficiently large. ∎

Another version of the above lemma is available, in a situation analogous to Lemma 3.1.

Lemma 2.3.

Let W~→𝜋W\widetilde{W}\xrightarrow{\pi}W be a desingularisation of a normal projective variety of dimension dd and ℱ\mathcal{F} be a coherent sheaf on W~\widetilde{W}. Assume that there exists an effective divisor EE on W~\widetilde{W} with π\pi-exceptional support, such that −E-E is π\pi-ample.

  1. (a)

    There exists a positive integer r0r_{0} such that such that Ri⁡π∗​ℱ​(−r​E)=0\RR^{i}\pi_{\ast}\mathcal{F}(-rE)=0 for all r≥r0r\geq r_{0} and all i>0i>0.

  2. (b)

    Suppose ℒ\mathcal{L} is ample on WW, and ℱ\mathcal{F} is locally free on W~\widetilde{W}. Then there exists a positive integer r1r_{1} such that for each r≥r1r\geq r_{1}, and for all n≥n1n\geq n_{1} (depending on rr), we have

    Hi​(W~,ℱ⁡(r​E)⊗π∗​ℒ−n)=0​ for all i<d,H^{i}(\widetilde{W},\mathcal{F}(rE)\otimes\pi^{*}\mathcal{L}^{-n})=0\;\;\;\mbox{ for all $i<d$},
    Hi​(W~,ℱ⁡(−r​E)⊗π∗​ℒn)=0​ for all i>0.H^{i}(\widetilde{W},\mathcal{F}(-rE)\otimes\pi^{*}\mathcal{L}^{n})=0\;\;\;\mbox{ for all $i>0$}.
Proof.

The assertion in (a) is just Serre’s vanishing theorem, since 𝒪W~​(−E){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{W}}(-E) is π\pi-ample. The two assertions in (b) are equivalent (with perhaps different values of r1r_{1}, n1n_{1}), using Serre duality on W~\widetilde{W}. The second assertion in (b) follows from (a), using the Leray spectral sequence for π\pi, and Serre’s vanishing on WW for the ample line bundle ℒ\mathcal{L}. ∎

We recall a form of the Grauert-Riemenschneider theorem which we need below.

Theorem 3.

Let WW be a non-singular projective variety over kk, and M\script M a big and base-point free line bundle on WW. Then Hi​(W,M−1)=0H^{i}(W,\script M^{-1})=0 for i<dimWi<\dim W.

Proof.

A proof of this statement can be found in [6], Cor. 5.6(b). ∎

3. Proof of Theorem 2

3.1. Some preliminary reductions

From now on, we fix the following notation (used in Theorem 2) – X~\widetilde{X} is a smooth projective kk-variety, ℳ\mathcal{M} a big line bundle on X~\widetilde{X}, V⊂H0​(X~,ℳ)\VV\subset H^{0}(\widetilde{X},\mathcal{M}) a subspace giving a linear system |V||\VV| without base points, Y~\widetilde{Y} a general member of this linear system, π:X~→X\pi:\widetilde{X}\to X obtained by Stein factorization of the morphism determined by |V||\VV|, Y~→Y\widetilde{Y}\to Y the induced morphism (which is also the Stein factorization of the restriction to Y~\widetilde{Y} of the original morphism on X~\widetilde{X}), and L\script L the invertible sheaf on XX such that π∗​L=M\pi^{*}\script L=\script M.

We first make a further reduction.

Lemma 3.1.

To prove Theorem 2, it suffices to do it in the case when the morphism π:X~→X\pi:\widetilde{X}\to X (obtained by Stein factorization) has a purely divisorial exceptional locus, with non-singular irreducible components, and there exists a π\pi-ample divisor of the form −E-E where EE is an effective divisor with π\pi-exceptional support.

Proof.

Since X~→X\widetilde{X}\to X and Y~→Y\widetilde{Y}\to Y are obtained from Stein factorizations of the morphisms determined by the base point free linear system |V||\VV|, we have that XX, YY are normal projective varieties, such that YY is a Cartier divisor in XX. There is an induced restriction homomorphism Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y).

It is easy to see that the conclusions of Theorem 2 hold for Pic⁡X~→Pic⁡Y~\Pic\widetilde{X}\to\Pic\widetilde{Y} if and only if the conclusions of Theorem 1 hold for Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y) (i.e., the restriction map on class groups is an isomorphism if dimX≥4\dim X\geq 4, and an inclusion with finitely generated cokernel if dimX=3\dim X=3).

In particular, if we replace X~→X\widetilde{X}\to X by another resolution of singularities π′:X~′→X\pi^{\prime}:\widetilde{X}^{\prime}\to X, and Y~\widetilde{Y} by the inverse image Y~′\widetilde{Y}^{\prime} of YY in that resolution, it suffices to prove Theorem 2 for this new pair (X~′,Y~′)(\widetilde{X}^{\prime},\widetilde{Y}^{\prime}), and the pull-back linear system from XX (note that there is an open subset of the linear system consisting of divisors which are “general” for both X~\widetilde{X} and X~′\widetilde{X}^{\prime}).

Now by Hironaka’s theorem, we can find a resolution of singularities π′:X~′→X\pi^{\prime}:\widetilde{X}^{\prime}\to X such that the exceptional locus is divisorial, with non-singular irreducible components. Further, there is an effective exceptional divisor EE such that −E-E is π′\pi^{\prime}-ample; this is because the resolution may be obtained by successive blow-ups at centres lying over the singular locus, so that the resolution may be viewed as a blow-up of an ideal sheaf whose radical defines the singular locus. The pull-back ideal sheaf is an invertible sheaf which is π′\pi^{\prime}-ample, and is the ideal sheaf on X~′\widetilde{X}^{\prime} of some subscheme with exceptional support. ∎

Remark 3.2.

This reduction is needed only in the proof that, if dimX≥4\dim X\geq 4, then Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y) is surjective.

We follow the line of proof of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem as given in [11]. The idea is to pass from Y~\widetilde{Y} to the formal completion 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} of X~\widetilde{X} along Y~\widetilde{Y}. Then from 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} we pass to a neighbourhood UU of Y~\widetilde{Y} in X~\widetilde{X}, using a version of the Lefschetz Conditions, and then to X~\widetilde{X} itself.

Lemma 3.3.

With notation as above, if dimX~≥4\dim\widetilde{X}\geq 4, then Pic⁡(𝔛)≅Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic({\mathfrak{X}})\cong\Pic(\widetilde{Y}). If dimX~=3\dim\widetilde{X}=3, then Pic⁡(𝔛)→Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic({\mathfrak{X}})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}) is injective, with finitely generated cokernel.

Proof.

Consider the short exact sequence

0→M−m⊗𝒪Y~→𝒪𝔛m+1×→𝒪𝔛m×→00\to\script M^{-m}\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}\to{\mathcal{O}}^{\times}_{{\mathfrak{X}}_{m+1}}\to{\mathcal{O}}^{\times}_{{\mathfrak{X}}_{m}}\to 0

where 𝔛m{\mathfrak{X}}_{m} is the mm-th infinitesimal neighbourhood of Y~⊂X~\widetilde{Y}\subset\widetilde{X} and in particular 𝔛1=Y~{\mathfrak{X}}_{1}=\widetilde{Y}. As usual, 𝒪T×{\mathcal{O}}^{\times}_{T} denotes the (multiplicative) sheaf of invertible regular functions on TT. The first horizontal sheaf map is the “exponential map”, defined on sections by s↦1+ss\mapsto 1+s. Taking the cohomology long exact sequence, one has

→H1⁡(Y~,M−m⊗𝒪Y~)→H1⁡(𝔛~m+1,𝒪𝔛m+1×)→H1⁡(𝔛m,𝒪𝔛m×)→H2⁡(Y~,M−m⊗𝒪Y~)→\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}{\scriptstyle\to}&{\scriptstyle\HH^{1}(\widetilde{Y},\script M^{-m}\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}})}&{\scriptstyle\to}&{\scriptstyle\HH^{1}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{X}}_{m+1},{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}_{m+1}}^{\times})}&{\scriptstyle\to}&{\scriptstyle\HH^{1}({\mathfrak{X}}_{m},{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}_{m}}^{\times})}&{\scriptstyle\to}&{\scriptstyle\HH^{2}(\widetilde{Y},\script M^{-m}\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}})}&{\scriptstyle\to}\end{array}

By the Grauert-Riemenschneider vanishing theorem (Theorem 3 above), the extreme terms vanish if dimY~≥3\dim\widetilde{Y}\geq 3, and thus we have Pic⁡(𝔛m+1)≅Pic⁡(𝔛m)\Pic({\mathfrak{X}}_{m+1})\cong\Pic({\mathfrak{X}}_{m}) for each m≥1m\geq 1. From the Grothendieck formula (see [10] II Ex. 9.6, for example)

Pic⁡(𝔛)≅lim𝑚⟵Pic⁡(𝔛m),\Pic({\mathfrak{X}})\cong{\displaystyle{\mathop{\rm lim}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0ptm}\limits^{\longleftarrow}}}}}\,\Pic({\mathfrak{X}}_{m}),

we then get Pic⁡(𝔛)≅Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic({\mathfrak{X}})\cong\Pic(\widetilde{Y}).

If dimY~=2\dim\widetilde{Y}=2, then the same argument shows that Pic⁡(𝔛m)→Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic({\mathfrak{X}}_{m})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}) is injective for each mm. On the other hand, H1​(X~,𝒪X~)→H1​(Y~,𝒪Y~)H^{1}(\widetilde{X},{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}})\to H^{1}(\widetilde{Y},{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}) is an isomorphism, since Hi​(X~,𝒪X~​(−Y~))H^{i}(\widetilde{X},{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-\widetilde{Y})) vanishes for i<3i<3 (Grauert-Riemenschneider vanishing, Theorem 3 above). Hence Pic0⁡(X~)→Pic0⁡(Y~)\Pic^{0}(\widetilde{X})\to\Pic^{0}(\widetilde{Y}) is an isogeny, and in particular is surjective. Hence Coker⁡Pic⁡(X~)→Pic⁡(Y~)\coker\Pic(\widetilde{X})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}) is a quotient of the Neron-Severi group of Y~\widetilde{Y}, and is finitely generated. A similar conclusion then clearly holds for Coker⁡Pic⁡(𝔛)→Pic⁡(Y~)\coker\Pic({\mathfrak{X}})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}). ∎

3.2. The condition Lef⁡(X~,Y~)\Lef(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y})

In the proof of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem (see [11], Ch. IV), one considers the Lefschetz condition which implies the injectivity of the morphism between the Picard groups. We will show that it holds in our situation as well.

If E\script E is a coherent sheaf on some open neighbourhood of Y~\widetilde{Y} in X~\widetilde{X}, then ^​E\widehat{\script}E denotes the corresponding (formal) coherent sheaf on the formal completion 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} of X~\widetilde{X} along Y~\widetilde{Y}. With this notation, recall the following definition (see [11], page 164; this is a slight modification of Grothendieck’s definition in [9], page 112, as remarked by the referee).

Definition 1.

The pair (X~,Y~)(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) satisfies the Lefschetz condition Lef⁡(X~,Y~)\Lef(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) if for every open set U⊂X~U\subset\widetilde{X} containing Y~\widetilde{Y}, and every locally free sheaf E\script E on UU, there exists an open set U′U^{\prime} with Y~⊂U′⊂U\widetilde{Y}\subset U^{\prime}\subset U such that the natural map

H0(U′,E|U′)→H0(𝔛,^E)\HH^{0}(U^{\prime},\script E_{|U^{\prime}})\to\HH^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\script}E)

is an isomorphism.

Note that there is a finite (perhaps empty) set S0⊂XS_{0}\subset X of (closed) points x∈Xx\in X with dimπ−1​(x)=dimX−1\dim\pi^{-1}(x)=\dim X-1. Since Y~\widetilde{Y} is general, we may assume that Y∩S0=∅Y\cap S_{0}=\emptyset. Further note that any divisor in X~\widetilde{X} whose support is disjoint from Y~\widetilde{Y} must be supported in π−1​(S0)\pi^{-1}(S_{0}). If EE is any divisor on X~\widetilde{X} with support in π−1​(S0)\pi^{-1}(S_{0}), then 𝒪X~​(E)^≅𝒪𝔛\widehat{{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(E)}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}}.

Recall that the dual of a coherent sheaf N\script N on X~\widetilde{X} is N∨=ℋ​o​m𝒪X~​(N,𝒪X~)\script N^{\vee}={\mathcal{H}om}_{{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}}(\script N,{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}); recall also that N\script N is reflexive if N→(N∨)∨\script N\to(\script N^{\vee})^{\vee} is an isomorphism.

Lemma 3.4.

Let N\script N be a reflexive, coherent sheaf on X~\widetilde{X} which is locally free in a neighbourhood of Y~\widetilde{Y}. Then there exists an effective divisor EE on X~\widetilde{X}, where either E=0E=0 or dimπ⁡(supp​E)=0\dim\pi({\rm supp}\,E)=0, such that the natural map

H0⁡(X~,N⁡(E))→H0⁡(𝔛,^​N)\HH^{0}(\widetilde{X},\script N(E))\to\HH^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\script}N)

is an isomorphism.

Proof.

Let n=dimX~n=\dim\widetilde{X}. Using Serre duality on X~\widetilde{X} and formal duality on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} (see [11], III, Theorem 3.3), we reduce to proving that

HY~n⁡(X~,N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)→Hn⁡(X~,N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)\HH^{n}_{\widetilde{Y}}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})\to\HH^{n}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})

is an isomorphism, for appropriate EE. Here, we note that though N\script N may not be locally free, Serre duality implies that the dual of the finite dimensional vector space Hn​(X~,N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)H^{n}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}}) is

Hom⁡(N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~,ωX~)=H0​(X~,N⁡(E)),{\rm Hom}(\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}},\omega_{\widetilde{X}})=H^{0}(\widetilde{X},\script N(E)),

since N\script N is reflexive.

For any effective divisor EE supported in π−1​(S0)\pi^{-1}(S_{0}), consider the commutative diagram with exact rows

Hn−1⁡(X~∖Y~,N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)→δ1HY~n⁡(X~,N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)↠Hn⁡(X~,N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)↓ϕ1↓ϕ2↓ϕ3Hn−1⁡(X~∖Y~,N∨⊗ωX~)→δ2OPENHY~n⁡(X~,N∨⊗ωX~))↠Hn⁡(X~,N∨⊗ωX~)\begin{array}[]{cccccccc}\HH^{n-1}(\widetilde{X}\setminus\widetilde{Y},\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})&\xrightarrow{\delta_{1}}&\HH^{n}_{\widetilde{Y}}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})&\twoheadrightarrow&\HH^{n}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})\\ \downarrow{\phi_{1}}&&\downarrow{\phi_{2}}&&\downarrow{\phi_{3}}&&\\ \HH^{n-1}(\widetilde{X}\setminus\widetilde{Y},\script N^{\vee}\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})&{\scriptstyle\xrightarrow{\delta_{2}}}&\HH^{n}_{\widetilde{Y}}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}}))&\twoheadrightarrow&\HH^{n}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})\\ \end{array}

The last maps in the sequences are onto since X~∖Y~\widetilde{X}\setminus\widetilde{Y} has cohomological dimension at most n−1n-1. Moreover, the map ϕ2\phi_{2} is an isomorphism by excision since Y~∩E=∅\widetilde{Y}\cap E=\emptyset. The Leray spectral sequence for the map π:X~∖Y~→X∖Y\pi:\widetilde{X}\setminus\widetilde{Y}\to X\setminus Y applied to the cohomology group Hn−1⁡(X~∖Y~,N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)\HH^{n-1}(\widetilde{X}\setminus\widetilde{Y},\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}}) has E2p,q=0\EE_{2}^{p,q}=0 for p>0p>0 (X∖YX\setminus Y is affine!). By Lemma 2.2, there exists an EE as in the statement of the lemma such that the map Rn−1⁡π∗​(N∨​(−E)⊗ωX~)→Rn−1⁡π∗​(N∨⊗ωX~)\RR^{n-1}\pi_{\ast}(\script N^{\vee}(-E)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})\to\RR^{n-1}\pi_{\ast}(\script N^{\vee}\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}}) is the zero map, and thus the map ϕ1\phi_{1} is the zero map, for this choice of EE. This in turn implies that the corresponding map δ1\delta_{1} is zero.

We thus have the following commutative diagram

HY~n⁡(X~,N∨​(−m​E)⊗ωX~)≅Hn⁡(X~,N∨​(−m​E)⊗ωX~)↓⁣≅↓HY~n⁡(X~,N∨⊗ωX~)↠Hn⁡(X~,N∨⊗ωX~)\begin{array}[]{ccc}\HH^{n}_{\widetilde{Y}}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}(-mE)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})&\cong&\HH^{n}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}(-mE)\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})\\ \downarrow{\cong}&&\downarrow\\ \HH^{n}_{\widetilde{Y}}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})&\twoheadrightarrow&\HH^{n}(\widetilde{X},\script N^{\vee}\otimes\omega_{\widetilde{X}})\\ \end{array}

Dualising, we have

H0⁡(X~,N⁡(m​E))≅H0⁡(𝔛,^​N)\HH^{0}(\widetilde{X},\script N(mE))\cong\HH^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\script}N)

∎

Corollary 3.5.

The condition Lef⁡(X~,Y~)\Lef(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) holds.

Proof.

For any open set U⊃Y~U\supset\widetilde{Y} in X~\widetilde{X}, and any locally free sheaf NU\script N_{U} on UU, we can find a reflexive sheaf N\script N on X~\widetilde{X} extending NU\script N_{U}, i.e., with N∣U≅NU\script N\mid_{U}\cong\script N_{U} (first choose a coherent extension, then replace it by its double dual). For a suitable divisor EE with dim(supp​E)=0\dim({\rm supp}\,E)=0, we have a commutative diagram induced by restriction maps

H0⁡(X~,N⁡(E))≅H0⁡(𝔛,^​N)↘↗H0⁡(U,N⁡(E))\begin{array}[]{ccc}\HH^{0}(\widetilde{X},\script N(E))&\cong&\HH^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\script}N)\\ \searrow&&\nearrow\\ &\HH^{0}(U,\script N(E))&\\ \end{array}

In particular, for any open VV such that Y~⊂V⊂U\widetilde{Y}\subset V\subset U and V∩supp​E=∅V\cap{\rm supp}\,E=\emptyset the above factorisation gives a surjection

H0⁡(V,N⁡(E))≅H0⁡(V,N)↠H0⁡(𝔛,^​N).\HH^{0}(V,\script N(E))\cong\HH^{0}(V,\script N)\twoheadrightarrow\HH^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\script}N).

But since N\script N is locally free on VV and VV is irreducible, the map is also an injection. Thus Lef⁡(X~,Y~)\Lef(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) holds. ∎

Corollary 3.6.

For normal XX, YY as above, the condition Lef⁡(X,Y)\Lef(X,Y) holds.

Proof.

Since XX and YY are normal, one has π∗​𝒪X~≅𝒪X\pi_{\ast}{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{X} and π∗​𝒪Y~≅𝒪Y\pi_{\ast}{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{Y}. Lef⁡(X,Y)\Lef(X,Y) then follows from Lef⁡(X~,Y~)\Lef(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) applied to sheaves which are pull backs of locally free sheaves on neighbourhoods of YY in XX. ∎

Corollary 3.7.

The kernel of the restriction map Pic⁡(X~)→Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic(\widetilde{X})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}) is freely generated by the classes of irreducible effective divisors which map to points in XX.

Proof.

It is obvious that the classes of such divisors are contained in the kernel since Y∩S0=∅Y\cap S_{0}=\emptyset (as YY is general). On the other hand, if 𝒩\mathcal{N} is a line bundle on X~\widetilde{X} with 𝒩⊗𝒪Y~≅𝒪Y~\mathcal{N}\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}, then we first note that 𝒩^≅𝒪𝔛\widehat{\mathcal{N}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}} by Lemma 3.3, and there is thus an invertible element of H0​(𝔛,𝒩^)H^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\mathcal{N}}); by Lemma 3.4, this formal global section is obtained from a global section on X~\widetilde{X} of 𝒩⁡(E)\mathcal{N}(E) for some divisor EE on X~\widetilde{X} supported over S0⊂XS_{0}\subset X. This section of 𝒩⁡(E)\mathcal{N}(E) has no zeroes when restricted to Y~\widetilde{Y}, so its divisor of zeroes E′E^{\prime} is also supported over S0S_{0}, and hence 𝒩≅𝒪X~​(E′−E)\mathcal{N}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(E^{\prime}-E). ∎

Corollary 3.8.

For each n≥0n\geq 0, and any effective divisor FF on X~\widetilde{X} with π\pi-exceptional support, the natural maps

H0​(X~,ℳ⊗n)→H0​(X~,ℳ⊗n​(F))→H0​(𝔛,ℳ⊗n​(F)^)H^{0}(\widetilde{X},{\mathcal{M}}^{\otimes n})\to H^{0}(\widetilde{X},{\mathcal{M}}^{\otimes n}(F))\to H^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{{\mathcal{M}}^{\otimes n}(F)})

are isomorphisms.

Proof.

Since M=π∗​L\script M=\pi^{*}\script L, where L\script L is invertible on the normal variety XX, and π∗​𝒪X~=𝒪X\pi_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}={\mathcal{O}}_{X}, it follows that M⊗n↪M⊗n​(E+F)\script M^{\otimes n}\hookrightarrow\script M^{\otimes n}(E+F) is an isomorphism on global sections for any effective divisor EE supported in π−1​(S0)\pi^{-1}(S_{0}), and any n≥0n\geq 0. ∎

3.3. The condition ALeff⁡(X~,Y~)\ALeff(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y})

We now introduce a second condition ALeff⁡(X~,Y~)\ALeff(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) (Almost Effective Lefschetz), which is a variation of Grothendieck’s Effective Lefschetz Condition (denoted by “Leff” in [11]). In the proof in [11] of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem, the condition Leff is used to show the surjectivity of the restriction map between the Picard groups; ALeff has a similar role here.

Definition 2.

We say the pair (X~,Y~)(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) satisfies the ALeff condition if

  1. (1)

    Lef⁡(X~,Y~)\Lef(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) holds and

  2. (2)

    for any (formal) invertible sheaf E\script E on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} there exists an open set UU containing Y~\widetilde{Y} and an invertible sheaf ℰ\mathcal{E} on UU, together with a map ℰ^→E\widehat{\mathcal{E}}\to\script E, which is an isomorphism outside the exceptional locus of π:Y~→Y\pi:\widetilde{Y}\to Y.

Note that the formal scheme 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} is a ringed space with underlying topological space Y~\widetilde{Y}, so the second condition above is meaningful.

For any formal coherent sheaf F\script F on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}}, we will make the following abuses of notation: for any divisor DD on X~\widetilde{X}, let F⁡(D)\script F(D) denote the formal coherent sheaf F⊗𝒪𝔛𝒪X~​(D)^\script F\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}}}\widehat{{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(D)}, and for any coherent 𝒢\mathcal{G} on X~\widetilde{X}, let F⊗𝒢\script F\otimes\mathcal{G} denote the formal coherent sheaf F⊗𝒪𝔛𝒢^\script F\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}}}\widehat{\mathcal{G}}.

Proposition 3.9.

Let X~\widetilde{X}, Y~\widetilde{Y} be as in Lemma 3.1, with dimX~≥3\dim\widetilde{X}\geq 3, and let EE be an effective divisor on X~\widetilde{X} with exceptional support such that −E-E is π\pi-ample. Then for any formal locally free sheaf F\script F on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}}, there exists r>0r>0 such that for any m≥0m\geq 0, if we set

Gm=F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m,\script G_{m}=\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m},

then for all m>>0m>>0,

Coker⁡(H0​(𝔛,Gm)⊗k𝒪𝔛→Gm)\coker\left(H^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\script G_{m})\otimes_{k}{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}}\to\script G_{m}\right)

is supported on Y~∩E\widetilde{Y}\cap E.

Proof.

The proof is in several steps. Let Fn=F⊗𝒪𝔛n\script F_{n}=\script F\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}_{n}}, for n≥1n\geq 1, be the sequence of locally free sheaves (on the sequence of schemes 𝔛n{\mathfrak{X}}_{n}) associated to the formal locally free sheaf F\script F. We have exact sequences

0→F⊗M⊗m−n→F⊗M⊗m→Fn⊗M⊗m→00\to\script F\otimes\script M^{\otimes m-n}\to\script F\otimes\script M^{\otimes m}\to\script F_{n}\otimes\script M^{\otimes m}\to 0

for each m∈ℤm\in{\mathbb{Z}} and n>0n>0, where the ideal sheaf of Y~\widetilde{Y} in 𝒪X~{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}} is identified with M−1\script M^{-1}.

Lemma 3.10.

Let d=dimY~d=\dim\widetilde{Y}. There exists r0>0r_{0}>0 such that, for each r≥r0r\geq r_{0}, all m>>0m>>0 (depending on rr), and all i>0i>0, we have

Hi​(Y~,F1⊗𝒪X~​(−r​E)⊗M⊗m)=0,H^{i}(\widetilde{Y},\script F_{1}\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})=0,
Hd−i​(Y~,F1⊗𝒪X~​(r​E)⊗M⊗−m)=0,H^{d-i}(\widetilde{Y},\script F_{1}\otimes{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes-m})=0,
Proof.

We have that M=π∗​L\script M=\pi^{*}\script L where L\script L is ample on XX. Now apply Lemma 2.3(b). ∎

Lemma 3.11.

There exists r0>0r_{0}>0 so that, for any r≥r0r\geq r_{0} and any m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z}, the vector space

H1​(𝔛,F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m)H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})

is finite dimensional.

Proof.

We have exact sheaf sequences

0→F1​(r​E)⊗M⊗m−n→Fn+1​(r​E)⊗M⊗m→Fn​(r​E)⊗M⊗m→0.0\to\script F_{1}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m-n}\to\script F_{n+1}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m}\to\script F_{n}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m}\to 0.

Since dimY~≥2\dim\widetilde{Y}\geq 2, we have for each given mm that

H1​(Y~,F1​(r​E)⊗M⊗m−n)=0H^{1}(\widetilde{Y},\script F_{1}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m-n})=0

provided n>>mn>>m, from Lemma 3.10; thus for n>>mn>>m,

H1​(𝔛n+1,Fn+1​(r​E)⊗M⊗m)→H1​(𝔛n,Fn​(r​E)⊗M⊗m)H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}}_{n+1},\script F_{n+1}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})\to H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}}_{n},\script F_{n}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})

is injective. Hence, in the Grothendieck formula

H1​(𝔛,F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m)=lim𝑛⟵H1​(𝔛n,Fn​(r​E)⊗M⊗m),H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})={\displaystyle{\mathop{\rm lim}_{\mathrel{\mathop{\kern 0.0ptn}\limits^{\longleftarrow}}}}}\,H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}}_{n},\script F_{n}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m}),

the maps in the inverse system on the right are, for n>>0n>>0, injective maps of finite dimensional kk-vector spaces (the above inverse limit formula holds, because the corresponding inverse system for H0H^{0} is an inverse system of finite dimensional kk-vector spaces, hence satisfies the Mittag-Leffler condition (ML)). Thus the inverse limit H1​(𝔛,F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m)H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m}) is a finite dimensional vector space. ∎

Now consider the exact sequences

0→F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m→F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1→F1​(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1→0.0\to\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m}\to\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1}\to\script F_{1}(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1}\to 0.
Lemma 3.12.

There exists r1>0r_{1}>0 so that, for each r≥r1r\geq r_{1}, and all m>>0m>>0 (depending on rr), the map

H1​(𝔛,F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m)→H1​(𝔛,F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})\to H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})

H1​(Y~,F1​(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)=0.H^{1}(\widetilde{Y},\script F_{1}(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})=0.

Fix an rr large enough so that the conclusions of Lemma 3.11 and 3.12 hold. Define

where the map is induced by the natural inclusion 𝒪X~​(−r​E)→𝒪X~​(r​E){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-rE)\to{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(rE), determined by the tautological section of 𝒪X~​(2​r​E){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(2rE). From Lemma 3.11, VmV_{m} is a finite dimensional vector space, and from Lemma 3.12, the natural maps

H1​(𝔛,F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m)→H1​(𝔛,F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})\to H^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})

induce surjections Vm→Vm+1V_{m}\to V_{m+1}, for all large enough mm. Hence Vm→Vm+1V_{m}\to V_{m+1} is in fact an isomorphism, for all large enough mm. Consider the commutative diagram of formal sheaves with exact rows

The vertical arrows are induced by the natural inclusion 𝒪X~​(−r​E)→𝒪X~​(r​E){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-rE)\to{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(rE) (as above, in defining VmV_{m}). There is an induced cohomology diagram with exact rows

H0⁡(𝔛,F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)→H0⁡(Y~,F1​(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)→H1⁡(𝔛,F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m)→H1⁡(𝔛,F⁡(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)↓↓α↓βm↓βm+1H0⁡(𝔛,F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)→H0⁡(Y~,F1​(r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)→H1⁡(𝔛,F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m)→H1⁡(𝔛,F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m+1)\hskip-56.9055pt\begin{array}[]{rccl}\HH^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})\to&\HH^{0}(\widetilde{Y},\script F_{1}(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})&\to\HH^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})\to&\HH^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})\\ \downarrow&\hskip 9.24994pt\downarrow\alpha&\hskip 9.24994pt\downarrow\beta_{m}&\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\hskip 9.24994pt\downarrow\beta_{m+1}\\ \HH^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})\to&\HH^{0}(\widetilde{Y},\script F_{1}(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})&\to\HH^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m})\to&\HH^{1}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1})\end{array}

Since Vm→Vm+1V_{m}\to V_{m+1} is an isomorphism, we see that
