contains the subspace

image​H0​(Y~,F1​(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1).{\rm image}\,H^{0}(\widetilde{Y},\script F_{1}(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1}).

Since m>>0m>>0, the global sections of the sheaf F1​(−r​E)⊗M⊗m+1\script F_{1}(-rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1} generate it on Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E (since the direct image of this sheaf on YY is globally generated, and Y~→Y\widetilde{Y}\to Y is an isomorphism outside Y~∩E\widetilde{Y}\cap E). Hence, the natural map between coherent formal sheaves

H0​(𝔛,F⁡(r​E)⊗Mm+1)⊗k𝒪𝔛→F⁡(r​E)⊗M⊗m+1H^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{m+1})\otimes_{k}{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}}\to\script F(rE)\otimes\script M^{\otimes m+1}

restricts to a surjection on Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E. This proves Proposition 3.9 ∎

Remark 3.13.

The referee has pointed out that, in Proposition 3.9, we can in fact get the stated conclusion for any integer rr, and all sufficiently large mm (depending on rr). Consider the pairs (r,m)(r,m) for which the conclusion of the Proposition holds. Given rr, we have seen already that there is a positive integer r0>rr_{0}>r so that (i) the conclusion holds for (r0,m)(r_{0},m) for all m≥m0m\geq m_{0}, say, and (ii) so that 𝒪X~​(−(r0−r)​E){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-(r_{0}-r)E) is very ample for π\pi. Then choose m1m_{1} so that π∗​𝒪X~​(−(r0−r)​E)⊗𝒪​Xℒ⊗m\pi_{*}{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-(r_{0}-r)E)\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}{X}}{\mathcal{L}}^{\otimes m} is globally generated for all m≥m1m\geq m_{1}. Then 𝒪X~​(−(r0−r)​E)⊗ℳ⊗m{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(-(r_{0}-r)E)\otimes{\mathcal{M}}^{\otimes m} is globally generated, for all m≥m1m\geq m_{1}. Hence the conclusion of the proposition holds for (r,m)(r,m) with m≥m0+m1m\geq m_{0}+m_{1}.

Proposition 3.14.

For X~\widetilde{X}, Y~\widetilde{Y} as above, the condition ALeff⁡(X~,Y~)\ALeff(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) holds.

Proof.

By Proposition 3.9, for any invertible formal sheaf F\script F on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}}, one has a map of formal locally free sheaves

(1) (^​M⊗−M)⊕s​(−F1)→F→0({\widehat{\script}M}^{\otimes{-M}})^{\oplus s}(-F_{1})\to\script F\to 0\hskip 14.22636pt

for some M>>0M>>0, s>0s>0, with cokernel supported in Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E, where F1F_{1} is an effective divisor on X~\widetilde{X} with exceptional support.

Similarly, for the dual formal line bundle F∨\script F^{\vee}, we have a map, sujective outside the exceptional locus,

(^​M⊗−N)⊕t​(−F2)→F∨→0(\widehat{\script}M^{\otimes{-N}})^{\oplus t}(-F_{2})\to\script F^{\vee}\to 0\hskip 14.22636pt

for some N>>0N>>0, t>0t>0. Dualizing this we have an injection

(2) F→(^​M⊗N)⊕t​(F2)\script F\to(\widehat{\script}M^{\otimes N})^{\oplus t}(F_{2})

which is a split inclusion on stalks at any point of Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E.

Composing the maps in (1) and (2), we have a map between formal locally free sheaves

(3) (^​M⊗−M)⊕s​(−F1)→τ^(^​M⊗N)⊕t​(F2)(\widehat{\script}M^{\otimes{-M}})^{\oplus s}(-F_{1})\xrightarrow{\widehat{\tau}}(\widehat{\script}M^{\otimes{N}})^{\oplus t}(F_{2})

such that Im⁡τ^↪F\im{\widehat{\tau}}\hookrightarrow\script F with cokernel supported in Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E.

The map τ^\widehat{\tau} may be described by an s×ts\times t matrix of elements of

H0​(𝔛,M^⊗N+M​(F1+F2)).H^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\script M}^{\otimes N+M}(F_{1}+F_{2})).

By the condition Lef⁡(X~,Y~)\Lef(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}) (or rather Corollary 3.8),

H0​(𝔛,M^⊗N+M​(F1+F2))≅H0​(X~,M⊗N+M),H^{0}({\mathfrak{X}},\widehat{\script M}^{\otimes N+M}(F_{1}+F_{2}))\cong H^{0}(\widetilde{X},\script M^{\otimes N+M}),

so that the map τ^\widehat{\tau} is the formal completion of a map of locally free sheaves on X~\widetilde{X}

(M⊗−M)⊕s​(−F1)→𝜏(M⊗N)⊕t​(F2).(\script M^{\otimes{-M}})^{\oplus s}(-F_{1})\xrightarrow{\tau}(\script M^{\otimes{N}})^{\oplus t}(F_{2}).

Thus we have Im⁡(τ)^↪F\widehat{\im(\tau)}\hookrightarrow\script F, with cokernel supported on Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E.

Now Im⁡(τ)\im(\tau) is a coherent sheaf on X~\widetilde{X}, such that for any point y∈Y~∖Ey\in\widetilde{Y}\setminus E, the stalk at yy satisfies

Im⁡(τ)y⊗𝒪X~,y𝒪X~,y^≅Fy≅𝒪𝔛,y≅𝒪X~,y^,\im(\tau)_{y}\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X},y}}\widehat{{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X},y}}\cong\script F_{y}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}},y}\cong\widehat{{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X},y}},

(where the completions are with respect to the ideal defining Y~\widetilde{Y}). Hence Im⁡(τ)\im(\tau) is a coherent sheaf of rank 1, which is invertible on X~\widetilde{X} at all points in Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E. Since X~\widetilde{X} is non-singular, the double dual of Im⁡(τ)\im(\tau) is an invertible sheaf F~\widetilde{\script F} on X~\widetilde{X}, such that

F~⊗𝒪Y~∣Y~∖E≅F1∣Y~∖E.\widetilde{\script F}\otimes{{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}}\mid_{\widetilde{Y}\setminus E}\cong{\script F_{1}}\mid_{\widetilde{Y}\setminus E}.

Thus we have ALeff⁡(X~,Y~)\ALeff(\widetilde{X},\widetilde{Y}). ∎

Remark 3.15.

The above argument, applied to an arbitrary formal locally free sheaf F\script F, implies the existence of a coherent, reflexive sheaf ℱ\mathcal{F} together with an injective map ℱ^→F\widehat{\mathcal{F}}\to\script F which restricts to an isomorphism on Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E. We do not know if ℱ\mathcal{F} can be chosen to be locally free in a neighbourhood of Y~\widetilde{Y}; perhaps the “natural” extension to our situation of the Grothendieck “Leff” condition is for this property to hold.

Corollary 3.16.

If dimX~≥4\dim\widetilde{X}\geq 4, the cokernel of the restriction map Pic⁡(X~)→Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic(\widetilde{X})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}) is generated by exceptional divisors of Y~\widetilde{Y} which map to points in YY.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.3 one has Pic⁡(𝔛)≅Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic({\mathfrak{X}})\cong\Pic(\widetilde{Y}). Let 𝒩\mathcal{N} be a line bundle on Y~\widetilde{Y}, and 𝔑\mathfrak{N} its unique lift to a formal line bundle on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}}. Proposition 3.14 implies that there exists an invertible sheaf 𝒢\mathcal{G} on X~\widetilde{X} such that 𝒢^≅𝔑\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\cong\mathfrak{N} on Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E. Thus 𝒢∣Y~⊗𝒩∨{\mathcal{G}}\mid_{\widetilde{Y}}\otimes{\mathcal{N}}^{\vee} is a line bundle on Y~\widetilde{Y} which has trivial restriction to Y~∖E\widetilde{Y}\setminus E, and is thus the line bundle associated to a divisor on Y~\widetilde{Y} with exceptional support. It remains to show that, upto tensoring with a line bundle restricted from X~\widetilde{X}, it corresponds to a sum of exceptional divisors for Y~→Y\widetilde{Y}\to Y with 0-dimensional image in YY.

Let E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} be the irreducible exceptional divisors of X~→X\widetilde{X}\to X, indexed so that for some 0≤s≤t≤r0\leq s\leq t\leq r, we have

  1. (i)

    E1,…,EsE_{1},\ldots,E_{s} are the irreducible divisors in X~\widetilde{X} with 0-dimensional image in XX

  2. (ii)

    Es+1,…,EtE_{s+1},\ldots,E_{t} are the irreducible divisors with 1-dimensional image in XX

  3. (iii)

    Et+1,…,ErE_{t+1},\ldots,E_{r} are the irreducible exceptional divisors for X~→X\widetilde{X}\to X whose images in XX have dimension ≥2\geq 2.

Since Y~∈|V|\widetilde{Y}\in|\VV| is a general member, we have

  1. (a)

    Y~∩Ei=∅\widetilde{Y}\cap E_{i}=\emptyset for 1≤i≤s1\leq i\leq s

  2. (b)

    for each s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t, let Y~∩Ei=∪j=1siFi​j\widetilde{Y}\cap E_{i}=\cup_{j=1}^{s_{i}}F_{ij} be the irreducible (equivalently connected) components of the intersection; then Y~∩Ei\widetilde{Y}\cap E_{i} is non-singular, reduced, and has no common irreducible component with Y~∩Ei′\widetilde{Y}\cap E_{i^{\prime}} for any i′≠ii^{\prime}\neq i

  3. (c)

    for t+1≤i≤rt+1\leq i\leq r, Fi=Y~∩EiF_{i}=\widetilde{Y}\cap E_{i} is reduced and irreducible.

Here, (a) is clear, and (c) follows from Bertini’s theorem. For (b), note that the linear system |V||\VV| restricts to a base-point free linear system |Vi||\VV_{i}| on EiE_{i}, and the Stein factorization of the corresponding morphism has the form πi:Ei→Ci\pi_{i}:E_{i}\to C_{i} for some irreducible curve CiC_{i}, such that |Vi||\VV_{i}| is the pull-back of a linear system from CiC_{i}. Hence the general member of |Vi||\VV_{i}| is a disjoint union of a finite set of fibers of Ei→CiE_{i}\to C_{i}, over points of CiC_{i} for which Ei→CiE_{i}\to C_{i} is smooth.

Thus, the line bundle determined by an irreducible exceptional divisor FF on Y~\widetilde{Y} lies in the image of the Pic⁡(X~)→Pic⁡(Y~)\Pic(\widetilde{X})\to\Pic(\widetilde{Y}), except possibly when FF is one of the Fi​jF_{ij} in (b) above, and the image of each such Fi​jF_{ij} in YY is a point. ∎

Lemma 3.17.

Assume dimX~≥3\dim\widetilde{X}\geq 3, and Y~∈|V|\widetilde{Y}\in|\VV| is general. Let FF be a divisor on Y~\widetilde{Y} with exceptional support, such that 𝒪Y~​(F){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(F) is the restriction of a line bundle from X~\widetilde{X}. Then there is a divisor F~\widetilde{F} on X~\widetilde{X} with exceptional support such that 𝒪X~​(F~)∣Y~=𝒪Y~​(F){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(\widetilde{F})\mid_{\widetilde{Y}}={\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(F).

Proof.

From the description of the irreducible exceptional divisors of Y~→Y\widetilde{Y}\to Y given in (a), (b), (c) of the proof of Corollary 3.16 above, we see that it suffices to assume (in the notation of (b)) that

(4) F=∑i=s+1t∑jni​j​Fi​j,F=\sum_{i=s+1}^{t}\sum_{j}n_{ij}F_{ij},

for some integers ni​jn_{ij}, s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t, 1≤j≤si1\leq j\leq s_{i}. Here, the divisors

Fi:=∑j=1siFi​jF_{i}:=\sum_{j=1}^{s_{i}}F_{ij}

for each s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t satisfy 𝒪X~​(Ei)∣Y~≅𝒪Y~​(Fi){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}}(E_{i})\mid_{\widetilde{Y}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(F_{i}).

So it suffices to show: if FF in (4) is such that 𝒪Y~​(F){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(F) is the restriction of a line bundle from X~\widetilde{X}, then ni​jn_{ij} is independent of jj, for each s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t. This is done using a suitable computation with intersection numbers.

Let T⊂X~T\subset\widetilde{X} be a general complete intersection of dimension 3, in some projective embedding of X~\widetilde{X}. Then by Bertini’s theorem, we may assume that

  1. (i)

    TT is irreducible and nonsingular, and the scheme theoretic intersection T∩EiT\cap E_{i} is a reduced, irreducible surface, for each 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r

  2. (ii)

    the scheme theoretic intersection Z:=T∩Y~Z:=T\cap\widetilde{Y} is a (reduced, irreducible) nonsingular surface in TT

  3. (iii)

    Z∩Ei=∅Z\cap E_{i}=\emptyset for 1≤i≤s1\leq i\leq s, and Z∩EiZ\cap E_{i} is a reduced, irreducible curve for each t+1≤i≤rt+1\leq i\leq r

  4. (iv)

    Z∩Fi​jZ\cap F_{ij} is a reduced, irreducible curve in ZZ, for each s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t, for all jj.

If T0T_{0} is the image of TT in XX, let T¯→T0\overline{T}\to T_{0} be the normalization. Then πT:T→T¯\pi_{T}:T\to\overline{T} is a resolution of singularities, such that T∩EiT\cap E_{i}, 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r are the irreducible exceptional divisors of πT\pi_{T}. The surface πT​(Z)=Z¯⊂T¯\pi_{T}(Z)=\overline{Z}\subset\overline{T} is a normal Cartier divisor in T¯\overline{T} (it is a general member of the ample, base-point free linear system on T¯\overline{T} determined by |V||\VV|). Let πZ:Z→Z¯\pi_{Z}:Z\to\overline{Z} be the restriction of πT\pi_{T}; then πZ\pi_{Z} is a resolution of singularities of a normal, projective surface, with irreducible exceptional curves Z∩EiZ\cap E_{i}, t+1≤i≤rt+1\leq i\leq r and Z∩Fi​jZ\cap F_{ij}, s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t, 1≤j≤si1\leq j\leq s_{i}.

Since the linear equivalence class of F=∑i,jni​j​Fi​jF=\sum_{i,j}n_{ij}F_{ij} is assumed to lie in the image of the restriction Pic⁡X~→Pic⁡Y~\Pic\widetilde{X}\to\Pic\widetilde{Y}, we have that 𝒪Z​(∑i,jni​j​Z∩Fi​j){\mathcal{O}}_{Z}(\sum_{i,j}n_{ij}Z\cap F_{ij}) is in the image of Pic⁡T→Pic⁡Z\Pic T\to\Pic Z. For each ii, the Fi​jF_{ij} are irreducible components of general fibers of Ei→CiE_{i}\to C_{i}. Hence Fi​j∩ZF_{ij}\cap Z are irreducible components of general fibers of T∩Ei→CiT\cap E_{i}\to C_{i}, and are thus algebraically equivalent as 1-cycles on the smooth projective 3-fold TT. Hence, for any divisor DD on TT, the intersection number (D⋅(Fi​j∩T))T(D\cdot(F_{ij}\cap T))_{T} is independent of jj, for each ii. Since Fi​j∩ZF_{ij}\cap Z is a Cartier divisor in ZZ, if DZD_{Z} is any divisor on ZZ representing 𝒪T​(D)∣Z{\mathcal{O}}_{T}(D)\mid_{Z}, the projection formula gives an equation between intersection numbers

(5) (DZ⋅(Fi​j∩Z))Z=(D⋅(Fi​j∩T))T(D_{Z}\cdot(F_{ij}\cap Z))_{Z}=(D\cdot(F_{ij}\cap T))_{T}

computed on the surface ZZ and the 3-fold TT, respectively.

Apply this to our divisor F∣Z=∑i,jni​j​Fi​j∩ZF\mid_{Z}=\sum_{i,j}n_{ij}F_{ij}\cap Z, which is assumed to be of the form DZD_{Z} for some divisor DD on TT. We get that

(6) (∑i​jni​j​(Fi​j∩Z)⋅(Fi′​j′∩Z))Z(\sum_{ij}n_{ij}(F_{ij}\cap Z)\cdot(F_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\cap Z))_{Z}

is independent of j′j^{\prime}, for each s+1≤i′≤ts+1\leq i^{\prime}\leq t.

Since Fi​j∩ZF_{ij}\cap Z are irreducible exceptional divisors for πZ:Z→Z¯\pi_{Z}:Z\to\overline{Z}, which is a resolution of singularities of a normal surface, the intersection matrix

(Fi​j∩Z,Fi′​j′∩Z)Z(F_{ij}\cap Z,F_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\cap Z)_{Z}

is negative definite. Regard (6) as a system of linear equations satisfied by the ni​jn_{ij}, with coefficients given by intersection numbers. The solutions of the system (6) for the “unknowns” ni​jn_{ij} correspond to elements in the ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-span of the Fi​jF_{ij}, which are in the orthogonal complement of the span of all the differences (Fi​j1∩Z)−(Fi​j2∩Z)(F_{ij_{1}}\cap Z)-(F_{ij_{2}}\cap Z), for all 1≤j1<j2≤si1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}\leq s_{i}, and all s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t. The span of these differences clearly has co-rank t−st-s, so the orthogonal complement has rank t−st-s. We have t−st-s elements ∑j=1si(Fi​j∩Z)\sum_{j=1}^{s_{i}}(F_{ij}\cap Z) which lie in the orthogonal complement, which are clearly independent, so must span the orthogonal complement after tensoring with ℚ\mathbb{Q}. This implies that FZ=∑i,jni​j​(Fi​j∩Z)F_{Z}=\sum_{i,j}n_{ij}(F_{ij}\cap Z) must be a rational linear combination of the divisors ∑j=1si(Fi​j∩Z)\sum_{j=1}^{s_{i}}(F_{ij}\cap Z), and so ni​jn_{ij} must be independent of jj, for each ii, as desired. ∎

Assume now that dimX≥4\dim X\geq 4. The conditions Lef\Lef and ALeff\ALeff imply that we have the following diagram, with exact rows and columns:

00↓↓0→IX′→ℤ⁡[EX]→ℤ⁡[EY]→IY′→0↓↓↓↓0→IX→Pic⁡(X~)→Pic⁡(Y~)→IY→0↓↓Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)↓↓00\begin{array}[]{ccccccccccc}&&&&0&&0&&&&\\ &&&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&&&\\ 0&\to&I_{X}^{{}^{\prime}}&\to&{\mathbb{Z}}[E_{X}]&\to&{\mathbb{Z}}[E_{Y}]&\to&I_{Y}^{{}^{\prime}}&\to&0\\ &&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\\ 0&\to&I_{X}&\to&\Pic(\widetilde{X})&\to&\Pic(\widetilde{Y})&\to&I_{Y}&\to&0\\ &&&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&&&\\ &&&&\Cl(X)&\to&\Cl(Y)&&&&\\ &&&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&&&\\ &&&&0&&0&&&&\\ \end{array}

Here ℤ⁡[EX]{\mathbb{Z}}[E_{X}] and ℤ⁡[EY]{\mathbb{Z}}[E_{Y}] are the subgroups in the respective Picard groups freely generated by the irreducible exceptional divisors in X~\widetilde{X} and Y~\widetilde{Y}, and IXI_{X}, IX′I^{\prime}_{X}, IYI_{Y}, IY′I^{\prime}_{Y} are defined by the exactness of the rows. Clearly IX′I^{\prime}_{X}, IY′I_{Y}^{{}^{\prime}} are generated by the irreducible exceptional divisors in X~\widetilde{X} and Y~\widetilde{Y}, respectively, which have 0-dimensional image under π\pi.

It is clear that IX≅IX′I_{X}\cong I_{X}^{{}^{\prime}}: it is an injection since ℤ⁡[EX]↪Pic⁡(X~){\mathbb{Z}}[E_{X}]\hookrightarrow\Pic(\widetilde{X}) is so. That it is a surjection follows from Corollary 3.7. Also Corollary 3.16 shows that that the map IY′→IYI_{Y}^{{}^{\prime}}\to I_{Y} is surjective, while it is also injective, by Lemma 3.17. Hence, from a diagram chase, we see that Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y) is an isomorphism, completing the proof of Theorem 2 when dimX~≥4\dim\widetilde{X}\geq 4.

By a similar argument, Corollary 3.7 and Lemma 3.17 imply that, if dimX~=3\dim\widetilde{X}=3, then Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y)\Cl(X)\to\Cl(Y) is injective. The finite generation of the cokernel results from the fact that Pic0⁡X~→Pic0⁡Y~\Pic^{0}\widetilde{X}\to\Pic^{0}\widetilde{Y} is an isogeny (and hence an isomorphism), since the map on tangent spaces H1​(X~,𝒪X~)→H1​(Y~,𝒪Y~)H^{1}(\widetilde{X},{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{X}})\to H^{1}(\widetilde{Y},{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}) is an isomorphism, from Theorem 3. This completes the proof of Theorem 2 in case dimX~=3\dim\widetilde{X}=3.

For possible use elsewhere, we make explicit the following result, more or less implicit above. We thank the referee for some illuminating remarks about formal Cartier divisors.

Theorem 4.

Let X~\widetilde{X} be as in lemma 3.1, with dimX~=3\dim\widetilde{X}=3, and let EE be an effective divisor on X~\widetilde{X} with exceptional support such that −E-E is π\pi-ample. Let Y~⊂X~\widetilde{Y}\subset\widetilde{X} be a general member of the linear system |V||\VV|, and let 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} denote the formal completion of X~\widetilde{X} along Y~\widetilde{Y}. Then the map

ρ𝔛:Pic⁡X~→Pic⁡𝔛\rho_{{\mathfrak{X}}}:\Pic\widetilde{X}\to\Pic{\mathfrak{X}}

has the following properties.

  1. (i)

    The kernel of ρ𝔛\rho_{{\mathfrak{X}}} is freely generated by the classes of irreducible π\pi-exceptional divisors with 0-dimensional image under π\pi.

  2. (ii)

    The cokernel of ρ𝔛\rho_{{\mathfrak{X}}} is generated by the classes of exceptional divisors FF on Y~\widetilde{Y} such that dimπ⁡(supp​F)=0\dim\pi({\rm supp}\,F)=0 (in particular, the corresponding line bundles on Y~\widetilde{Y} do extend to formal line bundles).

  3. (iii)

    With the notation introduced above (proof of Corollary 3.16), let AA denote the quotient of the free abelian group on Fi​jF_{ij}, s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t, 1≤j≤si1\leq j\leq s_{i}, by the subgroup generated by ∑j=1siFi​j\sum_{j=1}^{s_{i}}F_{ij}, for s+1≤i≤ts+1\leq i\leq t. Then there is a natural isomorphism Coker⁡(ρ𝔛)≅A\coker(\rho_{{\mathfrak{X}}})\cong A.

  4. (iv)

    Let π:X~→X\pi:\widetilde{X}\to X, π:Y~→Y\pi:\widetilde{Y}\to Y be the Stein factorizations. There is a natural isomorphism

    Coker⁡(Cl⁡(X)→Cl⁡(Y))≅Coker⁡(Pic⁡(𝔛)→Pic⁡(Y~)).\coker({\rm Cl}\,(X)\to{\rm Cl}\,(Y))\cong\coker({\rm Pic}\,({\mathfrak{X}})\to{\rm Pic}\,(\widetilde{Y})).

Most of these conclusions have already been obtained in the course of the above proof. The only remaining assertion to prove is that all the line bundles 𝒪Y~​(Fi​j){\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}(F_{ij}) do extend to formal line bundles on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}}. We thank the referee for suggesting a proof.

In fact, for each ii as in (iii), the divisor EiE_{i} defines a formal Cartier divisor Ei^\widehat{E_{i}} on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} with support Ei∩Y~E_{i}\cap\widetilde{Y}, which is a disjoint union of the closed sets Fi​jF_{ij}, 1≤j≤si1\leq j\leq s_{i}. Hence each connected component of the support defines a formal Cartier divisor Fi​j^\widehat{F_{ij}} on 𝔛{\mathfrak{X}} (one may first check a similar assertion for Cartier divisors on each of the schemes 𝔛m{\mathfrak{X}}_{m}, all of which have reduced scheme Y~\widetilde{Y}, for example). The associated formal line bundles are the desired extensions.

4. Application to 11-motives

In [4], §10, Deligne defined 1-motives over kk as complexes [L→G][L\to G], where LL is a lattice (free abelian group of finite rank with a continuous action of the absolute Galois group of kk), and GG a semi-abelian kk-variety. This gives an algebraic way of “defining” certain (co)homology groups of a variety, in a manner analogous to the way in which the Jacobian of a non-singular projective curve “defines” its first (co)homology group algebraically. Over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, 1-motives have a transcendental description using certain special types of mixed Hodge structures, and there is an equivalence of categories between 1-motives over ℂ{\mathbb{C}} and the full subcategory of these special types of mixed Hodge structures. In particular, there is an underlying philosophy (“Deligne’s Conjecture”, some aspects of which have been proved in [1], [14]) that, if one can construct a 1-motive transcendentally using some “part” of the mixed Hodge structure of an algebraic variety, then there must be an algebraic construction of that 1-motive as well, valid over more general ground fields. Further, if some operation between 1-motives can be constructed transcendentally, there must be an algebraic construction of it as well, and properties of such an operation (e.g. injectivity, isomorphism) should have algebraic proofs.

In [2], a 1-motive Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(X), the cohomological Albanese 1-motive, has been associated to any variety XX over a field kk of characteristic 0. If XX is proper, this is a semi-abelian variety over kk, and if XX is also non-singular, it coincides with the “classical” Albanese variety. If k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}, Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(X) can be constructed analytically, using the mixed Hodge structure on H2​n−1​(X,ℤ​(n))H^{2n-1}(X,{\mathbb{Z}}(n)), where n=dimXn=\dim X, in a manner generalizing the analytic construction of the Albanese variety of a non-singular proper complex variety. For a proper, possibly singular complex variety XX, one has a formula

Alb+⁡(X)​(ℂ)=Ext𝐌𝐇𝐒1⁡(ℤ,H2​n−1​(X,ℤ⁡(n)))\Alb^{+}(X)({\mathbb{C}})=\Ext^{1}_{\bf MHS}({\mathbb{Z}},H^{2n-1}(X,{\mathbb{Z}}(n)))

where the right side is the group of extensions in the (abelian) category of mixed Hodge structures.

If XX is projective, Y⊂XY\subset X is a (reduced, effective) Cartier divisor, then there is a Gysin map Alb+⁡(Y)→Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(Y)\to\Alb^{+}(X), constructed algebraically in [2], and which in case k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}} corresponds to the Gysin map (modulo torsion) H2​n−3​(Y,ℤ⁡(n−1))→H2​n−1​(X,ℤ⁡(n))H^{2n-3}(Y,{\mathbb{Z}}(n-1))\to H^{2n-1}(X,{\mathbb{Z}}(n)) in topology (which is a morphism of mixed Hodge structures).

In case XX is projective over ℂ{\mathbb{C}}, and YY is a general hyperplane section (here, “general” means “in a Zariski open set of the parameter variety”), then it is shown in [3] that Alb+⁡(Y)→Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(Y)\to\Alb^{+}(X) is an isomorphism when dimX=n≥3\dim X=n\geq 3; this is an important step in the proof of the Roitman theorem for singular projective complex varieties (the main result of [3]). In case XX (and hence YY) is non-singular, this is a particular case of the Lefschetz hyperplane theorem. The proof of this isomorphism in [3] is transcendental, ultimately relying on the local structure (in the Euclidean topology) of a morphism of complex varieties, which is given by the theory of Whitney stratifications (see [15], or [8], for example).

This suggests that, if XX is projective over a field kk of characteristic 0, of dimension ≥3\geq 3, and Y⊂XY\subset X is a general hyperplane section, then the Gysin map Alb+⁡(Y)→Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(Y)\to\Alb^{+}(X) is an isomorphism; further, the “philosophy of 1-motives” suggests that there is a purely algebraic proof of this fact.

The validity of the isomorphism over an arbitrary kk of characteristic 0 can be deduced from the case k=ℂk={\mathbb{C}}. An algebraic proof, on the other hand, can be obtained as follows.

It is easy to see that the general case follows from the case when kk is algebraically closed, so we assume this holds. Next, the category of 1-motives admits a notion of Cartier duality, which is an auto-antiequivalence of the category. So it suffices to show that the Cartier dual to Alb+⁡(Y)→Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(Y)\to\Alb^{+}(X) is an isomorphism.

It is shown in [2] that the Cartier dual of Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(X) is another 1-motive, explicitly described as follows (implicitly, this gives an algebraic description of Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(X)).

Let π:X′→X\pi:X^{\prime}\to X be the normalization map, Cl⁡(X′)\Cl(X^{\prime}) the divisor class group of the normal projective variety X′X^{\prime}, and Cl0⁡(X′)\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime}) the largest divisible subgroup. Then Cl0⁡(X′)\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime}) is naturally identified with (the kk-points of) an abelian variety (which can be identified with the Picard variety of any resolution of singularities). Let LXL_{X} denote the group of all Weil divisors DD on X′X^{\prime} such that

  1. (i)

    π∗​(D)=0\pi_{*}(D)=0 as a cycle on XX

  2. (ii)

    [D]∈Cl⁡(X)[D]\in\Cl(X) lies in the subgroup Cl0⁡(X′)\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime}).

If Div⁡(X′/X){\rm Div}(X^{\prime}/X) denotes the group of Weil divisors DD on X′X^{\prime} with π∗​(D)=0\pi_{*}(D)=0 as a cycle on XX, then

(7) LX=ker⁡(Div⁡(X′/X)→Cl⁡(X′)/Cl0⁡(X′)).L_{X}=\ker\left(\Div(X^{\prime}/X)\to\Cl(X^{\prime})/\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime})\right).

Note that Div⁡(X′/X){\rm Div}(X^{\prime}/X) is a subgroup of the group of Weil divisors on X′X^{\prime} which are supported on π−1​(Xs​i​n​g)\pi^{-1}(X_{sing}); in particular, Div⁡(X′/X)\Div(X^{\prime}/X) is free abelian of finite rank. Thus LXL_{X} is a free abelian group of finite rank, and the obvious homomorphism LX→Cl0⁡(X′)L_{X}\to\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime}) defines a 1-motive; this is the Cartier dual to Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(X).

We are given that YY is a general hyperplane section of XX in a certain projective embedding; the pull-back of the corresponding very ample linear system to X′X^{\prime} gives an ample, base-point free linear system on X′X^{\prime}. Hence Y′=Y×XX′Y^{\prime}=Y\times_{X}X^{\prime} is a general member of this linear system on X′X^{\prime}, and is thus normal, by Bertini’s theorem, so that Y′→YY^{\prime}\to Y is the normalization of YY. There is also an associated restriction map Cl⁡(X′)→Cl⁡(Y′)\Cl(X^{\prime})\to\Cl(Y^{\prime}), such that by Theorem 1 above, it is an isomorphism when n=dimX≥4n=\dim X\geq 4, and is an injection with finitely generated cokernel if n=3n=3. Hence it induces an isomorphism Cl0⁡(X′)→Cl0⁡(Y′)\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime})\to\Cl^{0}(Y^{\prime}) between abelian varieties, and an inclusion on quotients Cl⁡(X′)/Cl0⁡(X′)→Cl⁡(Y′)/Cl0⁡(Y′)\Cl(X^{\prime})/\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime})\to\Cl(Y^{\prime})/\Cl^{0}(Y^{\prime}), if dimX≥3\dim X\geq 3.

Now the Gysin map Alb+⁡(Y)→Alb+⁡(X)\Alb^{+}(Y)\to\Alb^{+}(X) is Cartier dual to a map of 1-motives (i.e., to a map between 2-term complexes)

[LX→Cl0(X′)]⟶[LY→Cl0(Y′)]\left[L_{X}\to\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime})\right]\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;\left[L_{Y}\to\Cl^{0}(Y^{\prime})\right]

where Cl0⁡(X′)→Cl0⁡(Y′)\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime})\to\Cl^{0}(Y^{\prime}) is the above isomorphism, induced by the restriction homomorphism Cl⁡(X′)→Cl⁡(Y′)\Cl(X^{\prime})\to\Cl(Y^{\prime}). It remains to see that, for general YY, this map is an isomorphism of 1-motives, i.e., the map LX→LYL_{X}\to L_{Y} is also an isomorphism.

Since Y′=Y×XX′Y^{\prime}=Y\times_{X}X^{\prime}, a functorial property of the refined Gysin homomorphism defined in [7] implies that if DD is a Weil divisor on X′X^{\prime} with π∗​(D)=0\pi_{*}(D)=0 as a cycle on XX, then the cycle [D∩Y′][D\cap Y^{\prime}] has the property that π∗​[D∩Y′]=0\pi_{*}[D\cap Y^{\prime}]=0 as a cycle on YY. This gives us a map LX→LYL_{X}\to L_{Y}. It is shown in [2] that this is the map corresponding to the Cartier dual of the Gysin map.

Since YY is a general member of a very ample linear system on XX, where dimX≥3\dim X\geq 3, it is clear (using Bertini’s theorem) that if DD is an irreducible Weil divisor in Y′Y^{\prime} lying over the singular locus of YY, then there is a unique irreducible Weil divisor D1D_{1} in X′X^{\prime}, lying over the singular locus of XX, such that D=D1∩Y′D=D_{1}\cap Y^{\prime} as divisors. This is because Ys​i​n​g=Xs​i​n​g∩YY_{sing}=X_{sing}\cap Y, giving a bijection between the codimension 1 irreducible components of Xs​i​n​gX_{sing} and Ys​i​n​gY_{sing}, which also gives a bijection between the codimension 1 irreducible components of π−1​(Xs​i​n​g)⊂X′\pi^{-1}(X_{sing})\subset X^{\prime} and π−1​(Ys​i​n​g)⊂Y′\pi^{-1}(Y_{sing})\subset Y^{\prime}. Hence, for general YY as above, we have that Div⁡(X′/X)→Div⁡(Y′/Y){\rm Div}(X^{\prime}/X)\to{\rm Div}(Y^{\prime}/Y) is an isomorphism. The formula (7) applied to XX and to YY, together with the fact (from Theorem 1) that Cl⁡(X′)/Cl0⁡(X′)→Cl⁡(Y′)/Cl0⁡(Y′)\Cl(X^{\prime})/\Cl^{0}(X^{\prime})\to\Cl(Y^{\prime})/\Cl^{0}(Y^{\prime}) is injective, implies that LX→LYL_{X}\to L_{Y} is an isomorphism, as was to be shown.

5. Some refinements, and statements in any characteristic

In this brief section, we make connections with the classical theory of Weil divisors, in the style of Weil [16] and Lang, as exposed in Lang’s book [12], following comments of the referee. This gives another perspective to the above results, and yields also some statements in arbitrary characteristic.

First, in Theorem 1, one can improve the statement in the following ways.

  1. (i)

    There is a dense Zariski open set Ω⊂|V|\Omega\subset|\VV| so that, if KK is any algebraically closed extension field of kk, XK=X×kKX_{K}=X\times_{k}K, and YK⊂XKY_{K}\subset X_{K} is a memeber of the base-changed linear system |V⊗kK||\VV\otimes_{k}K| on XKX_{K}, corresponding to a KK-point of Ω\Omega, then the theorem holds for the pair (XK,YK)(X_{K},Y_{K}). As stated, Theorem 1 does yield such an open subset of |V⊗kK||\VV\otimes_{k}K|, but in fact it may be taken to be ΩK\Omega_{K}. It is not difficult to modify the proof given above to yield this conclusion as well.

  2. (ii)

    When dimX=3\dim X=3, the cokernel of the (injective) map on class groups is in fact torsion-free. This follows from the proof given, since from Theorem 4, it boils down to the assertions that the cokernel of Pic⁡𝔛→Pic⁡Y~\Pic{\mathfrak{X}}\to\Pic\widetilde{Y} is torsion-free. If 𝒦=ker⁡(𝒪𝔛∗→𝒪Y~∗){\mathcal{K}}=\ker({\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathfrak{X}}}^{*}\to{\mathcal{O}}_{\widetilde{Y}}^{*}), then 𝒦\mathcal{K} is a sheaf of ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector spaces on the topological space Y~\widetilde{Y} (as may be immediately verified on suitable affine open subsets), and we have an exact sequence

    Pic⁡𝔛→Pic⁡Y~→H2​(Y~,𝒦)\Pic{\mathfrak{X}}\to\Pic\widetilde{Y}\to H^{2}(\widetilde{Y},{\mathcal{K}})

    where the last term is a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-vector space.

A different way of seeing (ii) is by a transcendental argument, using a suitable Lefschetz theorem, as in the Appendix: in Theorem 7, for i=n^i=\widehat{n}, the cokernel is torsion-free and the conclusions of that theorem also hold for cohomology with ℤ/n​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/n{\mathbb{Z}} coefficients, for any n>0n>0.

The referee has also pointed out that for a geometrically integral projective variety XX over a field kk, which is smooth in codimension 1, one can associate to it an abelian kk-variety PicW⁡(X)\Pic_{W}(X) (the “Picard variety in the sense of Weil”), such that when k=k¯k=\overline{k}, the group of kk-rational points PicW⁡(X)​(k)\Pic_{W}(X)(k) coincides with the group Cl0​(X){\rm Cl}^{0}(X), the maximal divisible subgroup of the group Cl⁡(X){\rm Cl}\,(X) of Weil divisors modulo linear equivalence. Further, the Weil-Neron-Severi group N​SW​(X)=Cl⁡(X)/Cl0​(X)NS_{W}(X)={\rm Cl}\,(X)/{\rm Cl}^{0}\,(X) is finitely generated. With this notation, we sketch the referee’s argument to prove the following result.

Theorem 5.

Let XX be an irreducible projective kk-variety of dimension d≥3d\geq 3, which is regular in codimension 1, where kk is an algebraically closed field of any characteristic. Let f:X→ℙkNf:X\to{\mathbb{P}}^{N}_{k} be an embedding. Let K¯\overline{K} be the algebraic closure of the function field K=k⁡(ℙ^kN)K=k(\widehat{{\mathbb{P}}}^{N}_{k}) of the dual projective space, and let YK⊂XKY_{K}\subset X_{K} be the generic hyperplane section. Then

  1. (i)

    PicW⁡(X)K→PicW⁡(YK)\Pic_{W}(X)_{K}\to\Pic_{W}(Y_{K}) is an isomorphism

  2. (ii)

    the composition

    N​SW​(X)→N​SW​(XK¯)→N​SW​(YK¯)NS_{W}(X)\to NS_{W}(X_{\overline{K}})\to NS_{W}(Y_{\overline{K}})

    is injective.

The isomorphism between Weil-Picard varieties is a consequence of [12] VIII, Theorem 4. The injectivity on Weil-Neron-Severi groups is reduced to a result of Weil [16]. We must show that, if ℒ\mathcal{L} is a line bundle on XX, whose pull-back to (YK)reg(Y_{K})_{\rm reg}, the smooth locus of YKY_{K}, is algebraically equivalent to 0, then ℒ\mathcal{L} is algebraically equivalent to 0 on XX. From [12] VI, Theorem 1, the pullback of ℒ\mathcal{L} to (YK)reg(Y_{K})_{\rm reg} determines a KK-rational point of PicW⁡(YK)=PicW⁡(X)K\Pic_{W}(Y_{K})=\Pic_{W}(X)_{K}. Since KK is a pure transcendental extension of kk, this must determine a kk-rational point of PicW⁡(X)\Pic_{W}(X). Hence, changing ℒ\mathcal{L} by the class of some point of PicW⁡(X)\Pic_{W}(X), we may assume ℒ\mathcal{L} has trivial pull-back to (YK)reg(Y_{K})_{\rm reg}. Now Theorem 2 of Weil [16] implies that ℒ\mathcal{L} is itself trivial on XX.

6. Appendix: Grothendieck-Lefschetz theorem for complex projective varieties

In this appendix, we shall sketch the proof of the following theorem using results from stratified Morse theory, as explained to us by Najmuddin Fakhruddin.

Theorem 6.

Let XX be a smooth projective variety of dimension at least 44 defined over the field of complex numbers, ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Let L\script L be a big line bundle over XX generated by global sections. If YY denotes a general member of the linear system |L||\script L|, then one has an exact sequence

0→K→Pic⁡(X)→Pic⁡(Y)→Q→00\to K\to\Pic(X)\to\Pic(Y)\to Q\to 0

where KK is the (free) subgroup generated by divisors in XX which map to points under the generically finite map X→𝜋ℙ⁡(H0⁡(X,L))X\xrightarrow{\pi}{\mathbb{P}}(\HH^{0}(X,\script L)) and QQ is the group generated by the irreducible components of the restriction of divisors in XX which map to curves under π\pi.

Theorem 6 is an immediate consequence of Corollaries 6.4 and 6.6 below.

In what follows, all cohomologies that we consider are singular cohomology of the underlying analytic space(s), with ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}-coefficients. Recall that, for any ℂ\mathbb{C}-variety, these cohomology groups support mixed Hodge structures, which are functorial for morphisms between varieties (see [4]). The proofs of Corollaries 6.4 and 6.6 are reduced to assertions about the homomorphisms Hi⁡(X)→Hi⁡(Y)\HH^{i}(X)\to\HH^{i}(Y) for i=1,2i=1,2, using the following standard lemma.

Lemma 6.1.

Let WW be a smooth proper ℂ\mathbb{C}-variety. Then there are isomorphisms, functorial for morphisms of ℂ\mathbb{C}-varieties,

Pic0⁡(W)≅H1​(W)⊗ℂF1​H1​(W)⊗ℂ+H1​(W),\Pic^{0}(W)\cong\frac{H^{1}(W)\otimes{\mathbb{C}}}{F^{1}H^{1}(W)\otimes{\mathbb{C}}+H^{1}(W)},
N​S​(W)=ker⁡(H2​(W)→H2​(W)⊗ℂF1​H2​(W)⊗ℂ).NS(W)=\ker\left(H^{2}(W)\to\frac{H^{2}(W)\otimes{\mathbb{C}}}{F^{1}H^{2}(W)\otimes{\mathbb{C}}}\right).
Proof.

From Serre’s GAGA, it follows that Pic⁡(W)≅Pic⁡(Wa​n)\Pic(W)\cong\Pic(W_{an}), where the latter denotes the group of isomorphism classes of analytic line bundles. Using the exponential sheaf sequence, and the Hodge decomposition, we obtain the above isomorphisms in a standard way, where Pic0⁡(W)=ker⁡(Pic⁡(W)→H2​(W))\Pic^{0}(W)=\ker(\Pic(W)\to H^{2}(W)) is the maximal divisible subgroup, and the Neron-Severi group NS⁡(W)=image⁡(Pic⁡(W)→H2⁡(W)){\rm NS}\,(W)={\rm image}\,(\Pic(W)\to\HH^{2}(W)) is finitely generated. ∎

We now state the following consequence of the Relative Lefschetz theorem with Large fibres (see [8], page 195).

Theorem 7.

Let WW be a nn-dimensional nonsingular connected algebraic variety. Let π:W→ℙN\pi:W\to{\mathbb{P}}^{N} be a morphism and let H⊂ℙNH\subset{\mathbb{P}}^{N} be a general linear subspace of codimension cc. Define ϕ⁡(k)\phi(k) to be the dimension of the set of points z∈ℙNz\in{\mathbb{P}}^{N} such that the fibre π−1​(z)\pi^{-1}(z) has dimension kk. (If this set is empty define ϕ⁡(k)=−∞.\phi(k)=-\infty.) Then the homomorphism induced by restriction,

Hi⁡(W,ℤ)→Hi⁡(π−1​(H),ℤ)\HH^{i}(W,{\mathbb{Z}})\to\HH^{i}(\pi^{-1}(H),{\mathbb{Z}})

is an isomorphism for i<n^i<\widehat{n} and is an injection for i=n^i=\widehat{n}, where

n^=n−s​u​p𝑘​(2​k−(n−ϕ⁡(k))+i​n​f​(ϕ⁡(k),c−1))−1\widehat{n}=~n-\underset{k}{sup}~(2k-(n-\phi(k))+inf(\phi(k),c-1))-1

In the situation of theorem 6, we first take W=XW=X, π\pi a generically finite map and HH a general hyperplane. Then one can easily check that n^≥1\widehat{n}\geq 1 in this case. Let X′X^{\prime} be the (open) subvariety of XX defined by removing all divisors which map to points under π\pi, and X′′X^{\prime\prime} be the subvariety obtained by further removing divisors which map to curves under π\pi. In these two cases, for the restriction of π\pi to X′X^{\prime} and X′′X^{\prime\prime}, one can check that n^≥2\widehat{n}\geq 2 and ≥3\geq 3 respectively.

Let Y=π−1​(H)Y=\pi^{-1}(H), and let Y′Y^{\prime} and Y′′Y^{\prime\prime} be defined similarly in X′X^{\prime} and X′′X^{\prime\prime} respectively. Since a general hyperplane section in ℙN{\mathbb{P}}^{N} misses points, one notes immediately that Y′=YY^{\prime}=Y.

Lemma 6.2.

If V⊂WV\subset W is a dense Zariski open subset of a non-singular proper variety WW, then

  1. (i)

    H1⁡(W,V)=0\HH^{1}(W,V)=0, and H2⁡(W,V)\HH^{2}(W,V) is a free abelian group, with a basis given by the irreducible divisors supported on W∖VW\setminus V (in particular, it is pure of weight 2)

  2. (ii)

    H3⁡(W,V)\HH^{3}(W,V) is a free abelian group, supporting a mixed Hodge structure with weights ≥3\geq 3.

Proof.

Let W∖V=DW\setminus V=D, and let S⊂DS\subset D be the union of the singular locus of DD, together with all irreducible components of DD of codimension ≥2\geq 2 in XX. Then D∖S=∐jDjD\setminus S=\coprod_{j}D_{j} where Dj⊂X∖SD_{j}\subset X\setminus S are irreducible, non-singular divisors.

We first observe that Hi⁡(W,W∖S)=0\HH^{i}(W,W\setminus S)=0 for i≤3i\leq 3, since S⊂WS\subset W has (complex) codimension ≥2\geq 2. This implies that Hi⁡(W,V)→Hi⁡(W∖S,V)\HH^{i}(W,V)\to\HH^{i}(W\setminus S,V) are isomorphisms for i≤3i\leq 3, Since (W∖S)∖V=∐jDj(W\setminus S)\setminus V=\coprod_{j}D_{j}, we have Thom-Gysin isomorphisms Hi(W∖S,V)≅⊕jHi−2(Dj)(−1)\HH^{i}(W\setminus S,V)\cong\oplus_{j}\HH^{i-2}(D_{j})(-1) for all i≥0i\geq 0 (where the Tate twist (−1)(-1) increases the weights by 2). In particular, we have Hi⁡(W∖S,V)=0\HH^{i}(W\setminus S,V)=0 for i<2i<2, H0⁡(Dj)=ℤ\HH^{0}(D_{j})={\mathbb{Z}} (the trivial MHS), and H1⁡(Dj)=Hom⁡(H1​(Dj,ℤ),ℤ)\HH^{1}(D_{j})={\rm Hom}\,(H_{1}(D_{j},{\mathbb{Z}}),{\mathbb{Z}}) is a torsion-free abelian group, which supports a MHS of weights ≥1\geq 1. ∎

Corollary 6.3.

H1⁡(X)≅H1⁡(Y)\HH^{1}(X)\cong\HH^{1}(Y).

Proof.

We have a factorization H1⁡(X)→H1⁡(X′)→H1⁡(Y′)=H1⁡(Y)\HH^{1}(X)\to\HH^{1}(X^{\prime})\to\HH^{1}(Y^{\prime})=\HH^{1}(Y), since Y=Y′⊂X′⊂XY=Y^{\prime}\subset X^{\prime}\subset X. By Theorem 7, we have that H1⁡(X′)→H1⁡(Y′)=H1⁡(Y)\HH^{1}(X^{\prime})\to\HH^{1}(Y^{\prime})=\HH^{1}(Y) is an isomorphism. In particular, H1⁡(X′)\HH^{1}(X^{\prime}) supports a pure Hodge structure of weight 1. Consider the exact cohomology sequence

H1⁡(X,X′)→H1⁡(X)→H1⁡(X′)→H2⁡(X,X′)→⋯\HH^{1}(X,X^{\prime})\to\HH^{1}(X)\to\HH^{1}(X^{\prime})\to\HH^{2}(X,X^{\prime})\to\cdots

By Lemma 6.2 with W=XW=X, V=X′V=X^{\prime}, we have H1⁡(X,X′)=0\HH^{1}(X,X^{\prime})=0, while H2⁡(X,X′)\HH^{2}(X,X^{\prime}) is torsion free, and it is pure of weight 2, generated by the cohomology classes of the irreducible divisors in X∖X′X\setminus X^{\prime}. Hence the boundary map H1⁡(X′)→H2⁡(X,X′)\HH^{1}(X^{\prime})\to\HH^{2}(X,X^{\prime}) is the zero map. Thus H1⁡(X)→H1⁡(X′)\HH^{1}(X)\to\HH^{1}(X^{\prime}) is an isomorphism. ∎

Corollary 6.4.

Pic0⁡(X)→Pic0⁡(Y)\Pic^{0}(X)\to\Pic^{0}(Y) is an isomorphism.

Proof.

The isomorphism in Corollary 6.3 is compatible with the respective Hodge structures, and so by Lemma 6.1, induces an isomorphism on Pic0\Pic^{0} groups. ∎

Proposition 6.5.

Let XX and YY be as in theorem 6. One then has an exact sequence

0→K→H2⁡(X)→H2⁡(Y)→Q→00\to K\to\HH^{2}(X)\to\HH^{2}(Y)\to Q\to 0

where KK (as in Theorem 6) is generated by divisors which map to points under π\pi and QQ is generated by the divisors in YY which map to points under π\pi.

Proof.

Consider the diagram:

(8) H1⁡(X)→a1H1⁡(X′′)→a2H2⁡(X,X′′)→a3H2⁡(X)→a4H2⁡(X′′)→a5H3⁡(X,X′′)↓ψ1↓ψ2↓ψ3↓ψ4↓ψ5↓H1⁡(Y)→b1H1⁡(Y′′)→b2H2⁡(Y,Y′′)→b3H2⁡(Y)→b4H2⁡(Y′′)→b5H3⁡(Y,Y′′)\begin{array}[]{cccccc}\HH^{1}(X)&\xrightarrow{a_{1}}\HH^{1}(X^{\prime\prime})\xrightarrow{a_{2}}&\HH^{2}(X,X^{\prime\prime})&\xrightarrow{a_{3}}\HH^{2}(X)\xrightarrow{a_{4}}&\HH^{2}(X^{\prime\prime})&\xrightarrow{a_{5}}\HH^{3}(X,X^{\prime\prime})\\ \quad\downarrow\psi_{1}&\quad\downarrow\psi_{2}&\quad\downarrow\psi_{3}&\quad\downarrow\psi_{4}&\quad\downarrow\psi_{5}&\quad\downarrow\\ \HH^{1}(Y)&\xrightarrow{b_{1}}\HH^{1}(Y^{\prime\prime})\xrightarrow{b_{2}}&\HH^{2}(Y,Y^{\prime\prime})&\xrightarrow{b_{3}}\HH^{2}(Y)\xrightarrow{b_{4}}&\HH^{2}(Y^{\prime\prime})&\xrightarrow{b_{5}}\HH^{3}(Y,Y^{\prime\prime})\\ \end{array}

Here the horizontal sequences are the cohomology long exact sequences corresponding to suitable pairs. The Proposition amounts to the assertions that there are isomorphisms

ker⁡ψ3→≅ker⁡ψ4,\ker\psi_{3}\xrightarrow{\cong}\ker\psi_{4},
Coker⁡ψ3→≅Coker⁡ψ4.\coker\psi_{3}\xrightarrow{\cong}\coker\psi_{4}.

From Theorem 7, ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ5\psi_{5} are isomorphisms, while ψ1\psi_{1} is an isomorphism from Corollary 6.3. We claim that ψ5\psi_{5} induces an isomorphism

image​a4→≅image​b4.{\rm image}\,a_{4}\xrightarrow{\cong}{\rm image}\,b_{4}.

This follows by an argument using weights. Let W2​H2⁡(X′′)⊂H2⁡(X′′)W_{2}\HH^{2}(X^{\prime\prime})\subset\HH^{2}(X^{\prime\prime}), W2​H2⁡(Y′′)⊂H2⁡(Y′′)W_{2}\HH^{2}(Y^{\prime\prime})\subset\HH^{2}(Y^{\prime\prime}) be the subgroups obtained as inverse images of the corresponding weight subspaces of cohomology with rational coefficients. Since ψ5\psi_{5} is an isomorphism of mixed Hodge structures, it induces an isomorphism W2​H2⁡(X′′)≅W2​H2⁡(Y′′)W_{2}\HH^{2}(X^{\prime\prime})\cong W_{2}\HH^{2}(Y^{\prime\prime}). By Lemma 6.2, H3⁡(X,X′′)\HH^{3}(X,X^{\prime\prime}) and H3⁡(Y,Y′′)\HH^{3}(Y,Y^{\prime\prime}) are torsion free, and have weights ≥3\geq 3, while H2⁡(X)\HH^{2}(X), H2⁡(Y)\HH^{2}(Y) are pure of weight 2. Hence we have

W2​H2⁡(X′′)=image​a4W_{2}\HH^{2}(X^{\prime\prime})={\rm image}\,a_{4}
W2​H2⁡(Y′′)=image​b4,W_{2}\HH^{2}(Y^{\prime\prime})={\rm image}\,b_{4},

and so ψ5\psi_{5} induces an isomorphism between these image subgroups.

Thus we have a commutative diagram with exact rows, and vertical isomorphisms as shown.

H1⁡(X)→a1H1⁡(X′′)→a2H2⁡(X,X′′)→a3H2⁡(X)→a4image​a4→0≅↓ψ1≅↓ψ2↓ψ3↓ψ4≅↓ψ5H1⁡(Y)→b1H1⁡(Y′′)→b2H2⁡(Y,Y′′)→b3H2⁡(Y)→b4image​b4→0\begin{array}[]{cccccc}\HH^{1}(X)&\xrightarrow{a_{1}}\HH^{1}(X^{\prime\prime})\xrightarrow{a_{2}}&\HH^{2}(X,X^{\prime\prime})&\xrightarrow{a_{3}}\HH^{2}(X)\xrightarrow{a_{4}}&{\rm image}\,a_{4}&\to 0\\ \cong\downarrow\psi_{1}&\cong\downarrow\psi_{2}&\quad\downarrow\psi_{3}&\quad\downarrow\psi_{4}&\cong\downarrow\psi_{5}\\ \HH^{1}(Y)&\xrightarrow{b_{1}}\HH^{1}(Y^{\prime\prime})\xrightarrow{b_{2}}&\HH^{2}(Y,Y^{\prime\prime})&\xrightarrow{b_{3}}\HH^{2}(Y)\xrightarrow{b_{4}}&{\rm image}\,b_{4}&\to 0\\ \end{array}

A version of the 5-lemma now implies that ker⁡ψ3→ker⁡ψ4\ker\psi_{3}\to\ker\psi_{4} and Coker⁡ψ3→Coker⁡ψ4\coker\psi_{3}\to\coker\psi_{4} are isomorphisms, as desired. ∎

Corollary 6.6.

There is an exact sequence

0→K→NS⁡(X)→NS⁡(Y)→Q→0.0\to K\to{\rm NS}\,(X)\to{\rm NS}\,(Y)\to Q\to 0.
Proof.

This follows from the Proposition, and Lemma 6.1, since the explicit descriptions of KK and QQ imply that K⊂NS⁡(X)K\subset{\rm NS}\,(X), and NS⁡(Y)↠Q{\rm NS}(Y)\twoheadrightarrow Q. ∎
